observability-metrics.core: Metrics are cheap, aggregatable numbers over time. Use counters, gauges and histograms (not summaries) for aggregatable latency quantiles; labels add dimensions but multiply series, so keep them bounded to avoid cardinality explosions; collect by pull for services and push for ephemeral jobs; and use exporters to translate systems that don't speak Prometheus.

first_principles.problem: Without good metrics, teams can't detect or size problems quickly.

analogy.title: A fleet dashboard
analogy.story: Gauges for every car, sliced by model and region.

check.q: What's the main risk when adding a new label to a metric?
check.a: Cardinality explosion if the label has many unique values, increasing memory and cost dramatically.

observability-logging.core: Modern logging centralises and structures logs from ephemeral containers. Use JSON fields instead of prose, meaningful levels, and injected context like trace_id. Node agents ship stdout reliably; Elasticsearch indexes everything for flexible search while Loki indexes labels cheaply; and sampling and deduplication keep volume and cost under control without losing errors.

first_principles.problem: Scattered, unstructured, noisy logs are useless in incidents and expensive.

analogy.title: A central record office with filing standards
analogy.story: Every record on a standard form, tagged and filed, with junk mail shredded.
analogy.breaks: Offices don't bill per page; log vendors do.

check.q: What three practices make logs most useful during incidents?
check.a: Structured fields, consistent levels, and injected context like trace_id for correlation.

observability-tracing.core: Distributed tracing reconstructs each request's path across services as a tree of spans sharing a trace_id. Context propagates in W3C traceparent headers through every hop, OpenTelemetry provides vendor-neutral instrumentation and export, events mark moments inside spans, and sampling (head for cost, tail for interesting traces) controls volume.

first_principles.problem: In microservices, nobody can see where a slow or failing request spends its time.

analogy.title: Parcel tracking across depots
analogy.story: Every scan logged, so delays are obvious.
analogy.breaks: Parcels take one route; requests fan out.

check.q: What breaks most often in real-world tracing deployments?
check.a: Context propagation: some hop (gateway, queue, async job) fails to forward traceparent, splitting traces.

observability-alerting.core: Alerting turns signals into human action. Page on user-facing symptoms rather than internal causes, write rules with expressions, a 'for' duration, ownership labels and runbook annotations, let Alertmanager deduplicate, group and route by team and severity, and use silences and inhibition plus regular pruning to prevent fatigue.

first_principles.problem: Noisy, ownerless alerts cause fatigue and missed outages.

analogy.title: A well-tuned check-engine light
analogy.story: Lights only for real problems, with a readable code and the right mechanic.
analogy.breaks: Cars have one light; services have many signals.

example.title: On-call week
flow: Delete cause alerts, add SLO burn alerts

check.q: Name two Alertmanager features that reduce alert noise.

slo-engineering-sli-slo-sla-error-budget.core: SLO engineering replaces 'as reliable as possible' with data. SLIs measure good versus valid user events; SLOs set realistic targets over windows; SLAs are looser external contracts; the error budget (1 − SLO) is the currency for risk with a policy for when it's exhausted; and multi-window burn-rate alerts page on budget consumption rather than raw thresholds.

first_principles.problem: Reliability debates are opinion-driven and alerts don't reflect user impact.

analogy.title: A household budget for failure
analogy.story: Know your allowance, track spending, tighten when overspent.
analogy.breaks: Money can be borrowed; budgets can't.

check.q: How do SLI, SLO and SLA relate?
check.a: The SLI is the measurement, the SLO is the internal target for it, and the SLA is the looser external contract with penalties.

promql-grafana-dashboards.core: PromQL queries labelled time series: select with matchers, transform counters with rate or increase (rate before sum), aggregate with by or without, combine with label-aware arithmetic and joins, and compute quantiles from histogram buckets. Grafana turns these into reusable dashboards with variables and annotations that correlate changes with metrics.

first_principles.problem: Wrong queries produce misleading dashboards and alerts.

analogy.title: Spreadsheet formulas over live readings
analogy.story: Filter, compute changes, roll up, and annotate events.

check.q: What are the three steps to compute a fleet-wide p99 from a histogram?
check.a: rate() the bucket counters, sum by le (and grouping labels), then histogram_quantile(0.99, ...).

observability-sampling-theory.core: Tracing at full volume is too expensive, so sampling selects what to keep. Head sampling decides cheaply at the root but is blind to outcome; tail sampling decides after completion to keep errors and slow traces but needs buffering and trace-ID routing; coherency requires the same decision for all spans of a trace; and hybrids combine early reduction with late selection.

first_principles.problem: Full tracing costs a fortune, and naive sampling loses the traces you need.

analogy.title: Smart CCTV retention
analogy.story: Keep incidents and samples, delete the rest, consistently across cameras.
analogy.breaks: CCTV has hindsight; head sampling doesn't.

check.q: Which sampling approach can guarantee keeping every error trace?
check.a: Tail-based sampling (with 100% of spans reaching the sampler), since it decides after seeing the outcome.

observability-pipeline-architecture.core: A telemetry pipeline sits between instrumented apps and backends. Agents collect and enrich at the edge; aggregators sample, redact, buffer and route centrally; the OTel Collector provides vendor-neutral receivers, processors, exporters and connectors; filtering and sampling cut cost; and routing sends each data type to the right tier or consumer. Fluent Bit, Vector and OTel fill different roles.

first_principles.problem: Direct-to-vendor telemetry is costly, inflexible and locked in.

analogy.title: A water treatment and distribution network
analogy.story: Collect, clean, then pipe to where it's needed.
analogy.breaks: Water is uniform; telemetry has varied value.

example.title: Platform pipeline
flow: Route: hot store, S3 archive, SIEM

check.q: What are the two main roles in a telemetry pipeline topology?
check.a: Agents (edge collection and light processing) and aggregators (central processing, sampling, routing and buffering).

network-performance-monitoring-npm.core: Network performance monitoring settles 'is it the network?' with data. Track latency percentiles, loss, jitter, utilisation and retransmits against baselines; active probes give continuous baselines from many vantage points, passive flows, eBPF and captures observe real traffic, and millisecond-resolution telemetry exposes micro-bursts that averages hide.

first_principles.problem: Network issues are blamed or dismissed without evidence.

analogy.title: Road sensors and traffic cameras
analogy.story: Test drives plus real traffic footage, at high speed.

example.title: Tail-latency mystery
flow: gNMI shows buffer drops at ToR

check.q: Why combine active and passive network monitoring?
check.a: Active gives constant baselines and early detection; passive shows what real traffic actually experiences.

observability-business-kpis.core: Business observability closes the 'all systems green' gap. Instrument outcomes like orders and revenue, map KPIs through journeys to services, quantify revenue at risk, use seasonal anomaly detection instead of static thresholds, and build shared dashboards that lead with business health and support it with technical SLIs.

first_principles.problem: Silent business failures go unnoticed while technical dashboards look fine.

analogy.title: Watching sales, not just tills
analogy.story: Working tills mean nothing if nobody buys.
analogy.breaks: Shops see empty floors; services need metrics.

example.title: Silent failure caught
flow: Breakdown: only card payments in DE

check.q: What kind of failure do business KPI alerts catch that SLO alerts may miss?
check.a: Failures where systems respond successfully but produce bad outcomes, like declined payments or broken marketing links.

observability-cardinality-explosion.core: Cardinality is the product of label values, multiplied further by histogram buckets and pod churn; one unbounded label can explode series counts, memory and bills. Detect culprits with TSDB status and per-label counts, then mitigate by dropping or normalising labels (moving detail to logs and traces) or aggregating before long-term storage.

first_principles.problem: Series explosions crash monitoring and inflate costs.

check.q: What are the two main mitigation strategies for cardinality explosion?
check.a: Remove or normalise the offending label, or aggregate away high-cardinality dimensions before storage.

observability-continuous-profiling.core: Continuous profiling samples stack traces in production at low overhead, revealing which code consumes CPU and memory. Sampling plus aggregation produces profiles; flamegraphs show cost as width; memory profiles separate allocation churn from retention and leaks; tools like Pyroscope and Parca store labelled profiles from SDKs and eBPF; and links to metrics, traces and deploys complete the picture.

first_principles.problem: Production-only performance issues can't be located at the code level.

analogy.title: An all-day fitness tracker for code
analogy.breaks: Trackers are personal; profilers cover fleets.

example.title: Cost win
flow: Fleet flamegraph: 18% CPU in logging serialization

check.q: Why is continuous profiling called the 'fourth pillar' of observability?
check.a: It adds code-level resource attribution that metrics, logs and traces don't provide.

observability-exemplars.core: Exemplars attach trace IDs to metric samples (one per histogram bucket, bounded in storage), carried via OpenMetrics or OTLP with exemplar storage enabled. Instrumentation adds them only for sampled traces, and Grafana shows them as clickable dots that open traces. They're the first link in a connected observability graph across metrics, traces, logs and profiles.

first_principles.problem: Metric spikes don't lead to concrete example requests.

analogy.title: Statistics with linked examples
analogy.story: Every number links to a real case.
analogy.breaks: Cases are curated; exemplars are automatic samples.

example.title: Setup checklist
flow: OTel SDK with trace_based exemplar filter

check.q: List the end-to-end requirements for exemplars to work.
check.a: Instrumentation attaching trace IDs (sampled), OpenMetrics/OTLP exposition, exemplar storage enabled in the backend, and a UI link to the trace store.

observability-ebpf-profiling.core: eBPF profilers sample stacks of every process from the kernel via perf-event timers and maps, giving zero-instrumentation, polyglot CPU profiles. Stack quality depends on frame pointers, symbols and runtime unwinders; off-CPU tracing covers waiting while SDKs remain better for memory; and always-on storage in Parca or Pyroscope lets you rewind incidents and diff versions.

first_principles.problem: Black-box and polyglot services can't be profiled with SDKs.

analogy.title: A building-wide thermal camera that records
analogy.story: See hot spots everywhere, and rewind.
analogy.breaks: Cameras need no symbols; profilers do.

check.q: What determines whether eBPF profiles show readable function names?
check.a: Availability of frame pointers or unwind info, debug symbols, and runtime support for JIT/interpreted languages.

observability-frontend-sre.core: Frontend SRE recognises that users experience the whole chain to their device. Measure with RUM (field, p75) and synthetics (lab, CI); target Core Web Vitals (LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness, CLS for stability); contain failures with error boundaries; make errors readable with private source maps; and build a stack of RUM, errors, synthetics, browser tracing and replay with frontend SLOs.

first_principles.problem: Fast backends still produce slow, broken user experiences.

analogy.title: Fast kitchen, fast waiters too
analogy.story: Service quality is judged at the table.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants have one table type; devices vary widely.

example.title: Performance program
flow: RUM shows LCP p75 4.6 s on Android

check.q: Name the three Core Web Vitals and what each measures.

observability-semantic-logging.core: Semantic logging turns logs into a consistent, typed event dataset. Agree an event catalogue with namespaced fields, types and units (building on OTel or ECS), make compliance easy with generated typed helpers and linting, carry trace and business-key context across sync and async hops, and query events across services like a database.

first_principles.problem: Inconsistent log fields make cross-service questions slow and unreliable.

analogy.title: One template for every department's records

check.q: What distinguishes semantic logging from merely structured logging?
check.a: A shared, enforced schema giving consistent event names, field names, types and units across services, not just JSON format.

observability-sre-chaos-engineering.core: Chaos engineering proves resilience by experiment. Define a measurable steady state with user-facing SLIs, hypothesise it survives a specific fault, inject realistic resource, state, network and latency faults with controlled scope and abort conditions using tools like Chaos Mesh or AWS FIS, and practise people and processes in GameDays with blameless reviews.

first_principles.problem: Resilience mechanisms fail during real incidents because they were never tested.

analogy.title: Fire drills for systems and teams
analogy.story: Find blocked exits while it's safe.
analogy.breaks: Drills don't harm; chaos needs safety controls.

check.q: What three elements define a well-formed chaos experiment?
check.a: A measurable steady state, a specific falsifiable hypothesis about a fault, and controlled scope with abort conditions.

opentelemetry-semantic-conventions.core: OpenTelemetry semantic conventions are the shared language of telemetry: versioned specs for resource attributes (who, including the golden trio of service name, version and environment) and operation attributes (what, for HTTP, DB, messaging and RPC), with types, units and requirement levels. Use generated constants to avoid typos, set schema_url, and migrate deliberately when conventions evolve.

first_principles.problem: Inconsistent attribute names fragment observability across services.

analogy.title: One building code for all builders
analogy.story: Anyone can work on any building.
analogy.breaks: Building codes rarely change; semconv does.

check.q: What's the difference between resource attributes and span attributes?
check.a: Resource attributes describe the telemetry producer (service, host, pod) for all signals; span attributes describe a specific operation.

sre-organizational-models.core: SRE is a practice of SLOs, error budgets, toil reduction and shared ownership, and team structure determines whether it works. Embedded SREs give depth to critical teams, platform SREs scale reliability through paved roads, consulting SREs spread expertise through time-boxed engagements, the kitchen-sink anti-pattern burns teams out, and hybrids tier models by service criticality.

first_principles.problem: Renamed ops teams don't deliver SRE outcomes.

analogy.title: A health system's staffing model
analogy.story: Specialists, public programmes and clinics, each where it fits.
analogy.breaks: Health systems are slow to change; SRE structures can adapt yearly.

example.title: Org evolution
flow: Grow: platform team with paved roads

check.q: Which SRE model scales best to many teams, and why?
check.a: Platform SRE, because shared paved-road infrastructure with built-in reliability serves all teams via self-service.
